title: A love letter to the 555 timer IC
summary: An affectionate note to the 555: eight pins, a century of hobbyist blinks, still teaching timing.

blocks.eyebrow: For the chip that blinked first
blocks.title: Dear 555,
blocks.body: You are not the fastest, the densest, or the most fashionable. You are the reason a thousand kitchen-table engineers learned what a timing capacitor feels like. This is a thank-you note disguised as a datasheet summary.

blocks.heading: Why anyone still cares
blocks.body: Hans Camenzind's 555 (introduced in the early 1970s) packed a comparator sandwich and a flip-flop into a friendly DIP. Astable mode blinked LEDs. Monostable mode debounced buttons. Students met thresholds at one-third and two-thirds VCC before they met microcontrollers. Fashion moved on; the pedagogy did not.

blocks.heading: The two moods everyone learns first

columns.name: Astable
columns.detail: Free-running oscillator. Charge and discharge a capacitor between thresholds — square-ish waves for days.

columns.name: Monostable
columns.detail: One-shot. A trigger pulse and you output a single timed high, then rest. Debounce, stretch, delay.

blocks.quote: You taught us that time is just a voltage climbing a curve.
blocks.attribution: Every lab partner who ever watched an electrolytic crawl toward 2/3 VCC

blocks.title: Still useful, still humble
blocks.body: Microcontrollers stole the glamorous jobs. The 555 kept the honest ones: a clean pulse, a teaching schematic, a part you can still buy when the supply chain jokes go quiet.
